title: How do five and nine pieces of one fourth look as rotis?
description: Five pieces and then nine pieces, each one fourth of a roti, are drawn and grouped into full rotis. Each group is written as an addition statement, in the way the half roti table was written.
teaching_notes: One idea: every four pieces of one fourth make one full roti, so counting the full rotis and the pieces left over names the amount. Watch for students who write four as the size of each piece.

source: Draw a picture and write an addition statement as above to show: a. 5 times 1/4 of a roti, b. 9 times 1/4 of a roti.
video_script.why: The child draws pieces that are each one fourth of a roti, groups every four into a full roti, and writes the amount as an addition statement.
video_script.substitution: Treat the pieces the way the half rotis were treated, but four pieces now make a full roti.
video_script.anchor: Five pieces and then nine pieces, each one fourth of a roti, grouped into full rotis
video_script.payoff_line: Five fourths make one full roti and one fourth more

final_answer.spoken: five fourths is one roti and one fourth more, and nine fourths is two rotis and one fourth more

video_script.fraction_reading: one fourth, five fourths, nine fourths
maths_rules: a roti cut into 4 equal pieces: each piece is 1/4, and 4 pieces make 1 full roti
5 x 1/4: 4 pieces make 1 full roti and 1 piece is left, so 5/4 = 1 + 1/4
9 x 1/4: 4 + 4 pieces make 2 full rotis and 1 piece is left, so 9/4 = 2 + 1/4
addition statement: 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 5 x 1/4, and nine 1/4 added = 9 x 1/4
video_script.design: One idea: group the pieces in fours to find the full rotis. Same method as the half roti table. The pieces stay on the board to the end.
